question: Which types of trailers can get stuck on raised railroad crossings due to low underneath clearance?
choice_a: Low-slung units such as a lowboy, car carrier, moving van, or possum-belly livestock trailer
choice_b: Tank trailers and reefers
choice_c: Flatbed trailers only
choice_d: Dry van trailers only
explanation: The manual lists low slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers as prone to getting stuck on raised crossings.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.4 - Railroad-highway Crossings

question: Besides low-slung trailers, what other tractor-trailer combination is noted as prone to getting stuck on raised railroad crossings?
choice_a: A tandem-axle tractor pulling a short trailer
choice_b: A single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with its landing gear set to accommodate a tandem-axle tractor
choice_c: A day cab pulling an empty trailer
choice_d: A bobtail tractor
explanation: The manual specifically warns about a single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with its landing gear set to accommodate a tandem-axle tractor.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.4 - Railroad-highway Crossings

question: If you get stuck on railroad tracks, what should you do first?
choice_a: Try to drive forward slowly
choice_b: Wait inside the vehicle for a train
choice_c: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks
choice_d: Rev the engine to build power
explanation: If for any reason you get stuck on the tracks, you should get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.4 - Railroad-highway Crossings

question: When calling 911 or the emergency number posted at a railroad crossing where you are stuck, what information should you give?
choice_a: Only your driver's license number
choice_b: Only the trailer's cargo manifest
choice_c: Your dispatcher's phone number
choice_d: The location using all identifiable landmarks, especially the DOT number if posted
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to give the location of the crossing using all identifiable landmarks, especially the DOT number if posted.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.4 - Railroad-highway Crossings

question: A skid where the rear wheels of a trailer lock up and the trailer swings around is often called what?
choice_a: A trailer jackknife
choice_b: A tractor jackknife
choice_c: A brake fade
choice_d: A rollover skid
explanation: When the wheels of a trailer lock up and it swings around, this type of jackknife is often called a 'trailer jackknife.'
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.5 - Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel vibrate
choice_b: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_c: Hearing a grinding noise
choice_d: The ABS warning light illuminating
explanation: The manual states the earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is by seeing it in your mirrors after applying the brakes hard.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.5 - Prevent Trailer Skids

question: To stop a trailer skid, what should you do with the brakes?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand brake firmly to straighten the rig
choice_b: Pump the brakes rapidly
choice_c: Release the brakes to get traction back
choice_d: Apply the parking brake immediately
explanation: The procedure for stopping a trailer skid is to release the brakes to get traction back on the trailer wheels.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.5 - Prevent Trailer Skids

question: Why is it wrong to use the trailer hand brake to try to 'straighten out' a jackknifing trailer?
choice_a: It will drain the air tanks too quickly
choice_b: It has no effect on the trailer at all
choice_c: It will engage the tractor protection valve
choice_d: The brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place
explanation: The manual explains this is the wrong thing to do since the brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.5 - Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is the term for the rear wheels of a vehicle following a different, narrower path than the front wheels when turning?
choice_a: Off-tracking (also called "cheating")
choice_b: Trailer sway
choice_c: Crack-the-whip
choice_d: Load shift
explanation: This is called off-tracking or 'cheating,' and it causes the path followed by a tractor to be wider than the rig itself.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.6 - Turn Wide

question: In a combination with more than one trailer, which unit's rear wheels off-track the most?
choice_a: The tractor's rear wheels
choice_b: The last trailer's rear wheels
choice_c: The first trailer's rear wheels
choice_d: All trailers off-track equally
explanation: If there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will off-track the most.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.6 - Turn Wide

question: When turning, why should you keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb even while steering the front end wide?
choice_a: It improves fuel economy
choice_b: It reduces tire wear
choice_c: It stops other drivers from passing you on the right
choice_d: It is required by DOT regulation
explanation: Keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb during a wide turn stops other drivers from passing you on the right.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.6 - Turn Wide

question: When backing a trailer, which direction do you turn the steering wheel to make the trailer go a certain way, compared to backing a car?
choice_a: The same direction as when backing a car
choice_b: It doesn't matter which direction
choice_c: You should not turn the wheel at all
choice_d: The opposite direction from backing a car
explanation: When backing a car, straight truck, or bus, you turn the top of the steering wheel in the direction you want to go; when backing a trailer, you turn it the opposite direction.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.7 - Backing with a Trailer

question: If you must back on a curved path, to which side should you back so you can see?
choice_a: The driver's side
choice_b: The passenger's side
choice_c: Either side, it makes no difference
choice_d: You should never back on a curved path
explanation: If you must back on a curved path, back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.7 - Backing with a Trailer

question: How should you correct drift when backing a trailer?
choice_a: Wait until you complete the maneuver, then correct
choice_b: Turn the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift, as soon as you see it
choice_c: Apply the trailer hand valve
choice_d: Speed up to regain control
explanation: As soon as you see the trailer getting off the proper path, correct it immediately by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.7 - Backing with a Trailer

question: What should you do if you need to reposition your vehicle while backing a trailer?
choice_a: Continue backing regardless of position
choice_b: Exit the vehicle and push the trailer by hand
choice_c: Make pull-ups to re-position the vehicle as needed
choice_d: Use the trailer hand valve to swing the trailer
explanation: When backing a trailer, make pull-ups to re-position your vehicle as needed.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.1.7 - Backing with a Trailer

question: What is the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar) properly used for?
choice_a: Normal driving braking
choice_b: Parking the trailer
choice_c: Releasing the tractor protection valve
choice_d: Testing the trailer brakes only
explanation: The trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes, not for driving or parking.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.1 - Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why should you not use the trailer hand valve while driving?
choice_a: It could make the trailer skid
choice_b: It uses too much air
choice_c: It is illegal in Tennessee
choice_d: It disengages the ABS system
explanation: Do not use the hand valve in driving because of the danger of making the trailer skid.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.1 - Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why should you never use the trailer hand valve to park a trailer that lacks spring brakes?
choice_a: It applies the brakes too hard
choice_b: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes
choice_c: It voids the manufacturer's warranty
choice_d: It could overheat the brake drums
explanation: Never use the hand valve for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes on trailers that don't have spring brakes.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.1 - Trailer Hand Valve

question: What does the tractor protection valve do if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak?
choice_a: It releases all air from the tractor system
choice_b: It applies the trailer's parking brake only
choice_c: It keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system
choice_d: It shuts off the engine
explanation: The tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.2 - Tractor Protection Valve

question: The tractor protection valve will close automatically when air pressure falls into approximately what range?
choice_a: 60 to 80 psi
choice_b: 5 to 10 psi
choice_c: 100 to 120 psi
choice_d: 20 to 45 psi
explanation: The tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.2 - Tractor Protection Valve

question: What color and shape is the trailer air supply control knob on newer vehicles?
choice_a: Red, eight-sided
choice_b: Yellow, round
choice_c: Blue, square
choice_d: Green, triangular
explanation: The trailer air supply control on newer vehicles is a red eight-sided knob used to control the tractor protection valve.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.3 - Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What happens when you pull out the trailer air supply control knob?
choice_a: It supplies air to the trailer and releases the brakes
choice_b: It shuts off the air supply and applies the trailer emergency brakes
choice_c: It charges the primary air tank only
choice_d: It disengages the parking brake
explanation: You push the knob in to supply the trailer with air, and pull it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.3 - Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What is another name for the service line on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: The supply line
choice_b: The emergency line
choice_c: The control line or signal line
choice_d: The dump line
explanation: The service line is also called the control line or signal line, and carries air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand valve.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.4 - Trailer Air-lines

question: The emergency air-line (also called the supply line) serves what two purposes?
choice_a: It powers the trailer lights and controls the horn
choice_b: It cools the brakes and lubricates the fifth wheel
choice_c: It only carries electrical signals
choice_d: It supplies air to the trailer tanks and controls the emergency brakes
explanation: The emergency line first supplies air to the trailer air tanks, and second controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.4 - Trailer Air-lines

question: Emergency lines are often color coded with which color to distinguish them from the service line?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Green
choice_c: Yellow
choice_d: Black
explanation: Emergency lines are often coded with the color red (red hose, red couplers) to keep from mixing them up with the blue service line.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.4 - Trailer Air-lines

question: What color is typically used for the service line couplers on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Orange
choice_b: Blue
choice_c: White
choice_d: Purple
explanation: Blue is used for the service lines and red for the emergency (supply) lines, to help avoid mistakes when coupling.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.5 - Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: When connecting glad hands, at what angle should the couplers be held to each other before joining?
choice_a: 45 degrees
choice_b: 180 degrees
choice_c: 90 degrees
choice_d: 0 degrees (parallel)
explanation: Press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90 degree angle to each other, then turn the glad hand to join and lock the couplers.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.5 - Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What part of a glad hand coupler prevents air from escaping?
choice_a: A metal gasket
choice_b: A wax ring
choice_c: A plastic cap
choice_d: A rubber seal
explanation: Glad hand couplers have a rubber seal, which prevents air from escaping; the seal and couplers should be cleaned before connecting.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.5 - Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: How often should you drain trailer air tanks to prevent water and oil buildup?
choice_a: Every day
choice_b: Once a month
choice_c: Once a week
choice_d: Only when the low-air warning activates
explanation: Each tank has a drain valve and you should drain each tank every day, even if it has automatic drains.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.6 - Trailer Air Tanks

question: Where should shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) be closed on a combination pulling more than one trailer?
choice_a: On the first trailer only
choice_b: At the back of the last trailer
choice_c: On every trailer in the combination
choice_d: Only on converter dollies
explanation: All shut-off valves must be in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.7 - Shut-off Valves

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Which trailers are NOT required to have spring brakes, per the manual?
choice_a: All trailers built after 1990
choice_b: Only trailers used for hazardous materials
choice_c: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975
choice_d: Trailers with ABS
explanation: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes; those without spring brakes rely on emergency brakes instead.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.8 - Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Why is it important to use wheel chocks when parking trailers without spring brakes?
choice_a: It is required by insurance policy only
choice_b: It prevents tire wear
choice_c: It is only a suggestion, not a safety issue
choice_d: The emergency brakes will hold only as long as air pressure remains, and it will eventually leak away
explanation: The emergency brakes on trailers without spring brakes hold only as long as there is air pressure in the trailer air tank, which will eventually leak away, so wheel chocks are essential.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.2.8 - Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: January 1, 1995
choice_c: July 1, 2000
choice_d: December 1, 1990
explanation: All trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.3.1 - Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Where is the ABS malfunction lamp located on a trailer?
choice_a: Yellow lamp on the right rear corner
choice_b: Yellow lamp on the left side, front or rear corner
choice_c: Red lamp on the dashboard
choice_d: Blue lamp on the roof
explanation: Trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.3.1 - Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten your stopping distance?
choice_a: Yes, always by half
choice_b: Yes, but only on wet roads
choice_c: No, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_d: No, ABS has no effect on braking at all
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.3.2 - Braking with ABS

question: How should you brake a tractor-trailer combination equipped with ABS compared to one without it?
choice_a: You should brake much more aggressively
choice_b: You should pump the brakes rapidly
choice_c: You should rely solely on the trailer hand valve
choice_d: You should brake the same way as you always have
explanation: When you drive a combination with ABS, you should brake the same way, regardless of whether you have ABS on the tractor, trailer, or both.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.3.2 - Braking with ABS

question: Before backing under a trailer, how should the fifth wheel be positioned?
choice_a: Tilted down toward the rear of the tractor, with jaws open
choice_b: Tilted up toward the front of the tractor
choice_c: Locked in the fully open uncoupled position with jaws closed
choice_d: Rotated 90 degrees from the trailer centerline
explanation: The fifth wheel should be tilted down toward the rear of the tractor, with the jaws open, before coupling.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: How should you position the tractor before backing it under the trailer?
choice_a: At a slight angle to allow easier alignment
choice_b: Directly in front of the trailer, never at an angle
choice_c: Off to one side to check clearance first
choice_d: With the tractor already coupled to another trailer
explanation: Put the tractor directly in front of the trailer; never back under it at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: What could happen if the trailer is too low when you back the tractor under it?
choice_a: Nothing, this is the correct height
choice_b: The kingpin will automatically adjust
choice_c: The tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose
choice_d: The landing gear will retract automatically
explanation: If the trailer is too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose; if too high, it may not couple correctly.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After supplying air to the trailer during coupling, how do you check the brake system for crossed air-lines?
choice_a: Look at the tire pressure gauge
choice_b: Check the transmission fluid level
choice_c: Inspect the mud flaps
choice_d: Shut the engine off, apply and release trailer brakes, and listen for the brakes moving and air escaping
explanation: Shut engine off so you can hear the brakes, apply and release trailer brakes, and listen for the sound of the brakes being applied and released.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: Before backing the tractor under the trailer, what should you do with the trailer brakes?
choice_a: Pull out the air supply knob (or move the control to "emergency") to lock them
choice_b: Leave them released
choice_c: Disconnect the air lines entirely
choice_d: Apply only the parking brake on the tractor
explanation: Step 9 instructs to pull out the air supply knob or move the tractor protection valve control from 'normal' to 'emergency' to lock trailer brakes before backing under.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After coupling, how do you check that the trailer is securely locked onto the tractor?
choice_a: Visually inspect from a distance only
choice_b: Raise the landing gear slightly and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are locked
choice_c: Drive at highway speed and brake hard
choice_d: Sound the horn and listen for an echo
explanation: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check the connection.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: What does it mean if there is visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel after coupling?
choice_a: This is normal and expected
choice_b: It indicates the landing gear needs lubrication
choice_c: Something is wrong; the kingpin may be on top of the closed jaws
choice_d: It means the air lines are crossed
explanation: If there is space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, something is wrong; the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws, and the trailer could come loose.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: Why should you never drive with the landing gear only part way up?
choice_a: It reduces fuel efficiency
choice_b: It causes the ABS light to illuminate
choice_c: It is only a cosmetic issue
choice_d: It may catch on railroad tracks or other objects
explanation: Never drive with the landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.1 - Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When pulling the tractor forward during uncoupling, where should you stop?
choice_a: With the tractor frame still under the trailer, to prevent it falling if the landing gear collapses
choice_b: As soon as the fifth wheel clears the trailer completely
choice_c: Only after driving at least 50 feet away
choice_d: With the trailer wheels off the ground
explanation: Stop with the tractor frame under the trailer, which prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.2 - Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: What should you check before operating a pintle hook coupling?
choice_a: Only the tire pressure of the towed trailer
choice_b: For worn, damaged, or missing parts, and that the mount is secure
choice_c: The trailer's cargo weight only
choice_d: The fuel level of the tow vehicle
explanation: Before operating, check the pintle hook for worn, damaged, or missing parts, and make sure the mount is secure.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.3 - Coupling a Pintle Hook

question: According to the manual, what does the law require for all trailers when coupling a gooseneck hitch?
choice_a: A backup camera
choice_b: A second set of brake lights
choice_c: Safety chains
choice_d: A spare tire mounted on the trailer
explanation: The manual states: 'Remember that all trailers are required by law to have safety chains.'
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.4.7 - Coupling a Gooseneck Hitch

question: How do you test the tractor protection valve during a combination vehicle brake check?
choice_a: Drive at highway speed and apply the brakes hard
choice_b: Disconnect the emergency line and listen for air escaping only
choice_c: Check the tire tread depth
choice_d: Charge the air system, shut off the engine, and step on and off the brake pedal until the control pops out at the specified pressure range
explanation: Charge the trailer air-brake system, shut the engine off, and step on and off the brake pedal until the trailer air supply control pops out (usually within 20 to 45 psi).
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.5.2 - Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: How do you test the trailer emergency brakes during a combination vehicle brake check?
choice_a: Charge the air system, check the trailer rolls freely, then pull out the air supply control and pull gently on the trailer with the tractor
choice_b: Apply the trailer hand valve while driving at speed
choice_c: Check the ABS malfunction lamp only
choice_d: Remove the wheel chocks and observe
explanation: Charge the trailer air brake system, check the trailer rolls freely, then pull out the trailer air supply control and pull gently on the trailer with the tractor to confirm the emergency brakes engage.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 6.5.2 - Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: What must you do to help prevent trailers from rolling over when pulling doubles or triples?
choice_a: Maintain highway speed through all curves
choice_b: Steer gently and go slowly around corners, ramps, and curves
choice_c: Use the trailer hand valve frequently
choice_d: Keep the shut-off valves closed on all trailers
explanation: To prevent trailers from rolling over, you must steer gently and go slowly around corners, on ramps, off ramps, and curves.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 7.1.1 - Prevent Trailer from Rolling Over

question: In the 'crack-the-whip' effect, which trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over?
choice_a: The first trailer
choice_b: The tractor itself
choice_c: The last trailer in the combination
choice_d: All trailers turn over equally
explanation: The last trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over because of the crack-the-whip effect.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 7.1.2 - Beware of the Crack-the-whip Effect

question: Why must drivers of doubles and triples allow more following distance?
choice_a: Because federal law requires it regardless of vehicle type
choice_b: Because their brakes are weaker than single trailers
choice_c: Because they lack mirrors
choice_d: Because these combinations take up more space and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly
explanation: Doubles and triples take up more space and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly, so drivers must allow more following distance.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 7.1.5 - Manage Space

question: Why should you be more careful with double and triple bottoms in adverse conditions?
choice_a: They have greater length and more dead axles, increasing the chance of skids and loss of traction
choice_b: They have fewer lights than single trailers
choice_c: They are not equipped with air brakes
choice_d: They cannot use ABS
explanation: Doubles and triples have greater length and more dead axles to pull with the drive axles, creating more chance for skids and loss of traction.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 7.1.6 - Adverse Conditions

question: For the safest handling on the road, which trailer should be placed in the first position behind the tractor?
choice_a: The lighter trailer
choice_b: The more heavily loaded semitrailer
choice_c: Whichever trailer was loaded first
choice_d: It does not matter
explanation: For the safest handling on the road, the more heavily loaded semitrailer should be in first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 7.2.1 - Coupling Twin Trailers

question: If the second (rear) trailer in a set of twins doesn't have spring brakes, how do you set its emergency brakes during coupling?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand valve only
choice_b: Chock the wheels and do nothing else
choice_c: Charge the trailer air tank, then disconnect the emergency line
choice_d: Leave the trailer uncoupled until departure
explanation: Drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, and disconnect the emergency line to set the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Tennessee CDL Manual, Section 7.2.1 - Coupling Twin Trailers
